What is the difference between a model parameter and a hyperparameter?
column2: A parameter is learned by the training algorithm (e.g. a weight). A hyperparameter is set by you before training and controls the learning process itself (e.g. regularization strength, learning rate). Only hyperparameters can be overfit to the validation set.

column1: What is sampling bias?
column2: When the training sample is not representative of the population you will deploy on, because of how it was collected. Classic example: the 1936 Literary Digest poll surveyed telephone and car owners and predicted the wrong US president despite 2.4 million responses.

column1: You see low training error, low train-dev error, but high validation error. What is wrong?
column2: Data mismatch — not overfitting. Your training distribution differs from your validation/production distribution. Fix the data, not the model.

column1: What does the No Free Lunch theorem actually claim?
column2: Averaged over all possible problems, no algorithm outperforms any other. Practically: every model embeds assumptions about the data, so there is no universally best model and you must evaluate empirically on your problem.

column1: What is self-supervised learning, and why does it matter for LLMs?
column2: Labels are generated from the input itself rather than annotated by humans — e.g. mask a token and predict it, or predict the next token. It is what allows training on internet-scale unlabeled text, and it is the objective behind every LLM pretraining run.

column1: Name the two categories of things that make an ML project fail, per Géron.
column2: Bad data (too little, unrepresentative, poor quality, irrelevant features) and bad algorithm (overfitting or underfitting the training data).

column1: Why fit transformers on the training set only?
column2: Transformer parameters (imputation medians, scaler mean/std, encoder categories) are learned. Fitting on all data leaks test-set statistics into training, producing optimistic and dishonest validation scores.

column1: RMSE vs MAE — when do you pick each?
column2: RMSE (ℓ₂) squares errors, so it penalizes large ones disproportionately — use it when errors are roughly Gaussian. MAE (ℓ₁) weights all errors linearly — use it when outliers exist and you don't want them to dominate.

column1: What is data snooping bias?
column2: Exploring the test set (or the full dataset) before splitting, so that your own model and feature choices are shaped by test data. Your brain overfits even when your code doesn't.

column1: A decision tree scores RMSE = 0 on training data. What does that tell you?
column2: It memorized the training set — severe overfitting. Confirm with cross-validation, where its error will be much worse than a properly regularized model's.

column1: GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV?
column2: Grid for small, discrete, well-understood spaces where you want exhaustive coverage. Random for large or continuous spaces — for a fixed compute budget it samples far more distinct values per hyperparameter.

column1: Why did rooms_per_household beat total_rooms as a feature?
column2: total_rooms for a district mostly encodes district size, not housing quality. Dividing by households turns a size proxy into a meaningful per-unit ratio. Feature engineering outperformed every model change in the chapter.

column1: Why is accuracy a bad metric for imbalanced classification?
column2: A classifier that always predicts the majority class gets high accuracy while learning nothing. On MNIST's 5-detector, "always not-5" scores 90%.

column1: Precision vs recall, in one line each.
column2: Precision = of what I flagged, how much was correct (TP/(TP+FP)) — the cost of false alarms. Recall = of what I should have flagged, how much I caught (TP/(TP+FN)) — the cost of misses.

column1: When should you prefer a PR curve over a ROC curve?
column2: When the positive class is rare, or when false positives matter more than false negatives. FPR's denominator includes the huge TN count, so ROC AUC stays optimistic on imbalanced data; PR has no TN term.

column1: How do you actually trade precision for recall?
column2: Move the decision threshold on the classifier's score. Higher threshold → fewer positives → higher precision, lower recall. Get scores with decision_function or predict_proba, then sweep.

column1: OvR vs OvO for multiclass — when is OvO preferred?
column2: OvR trains N classifiers on the full dataset. OvO trains N(N−1)/2 classifiers, each on only two classes' data. Prefer OvO when the algorithm scales badly with dataset size — notably SVMs.

column1: What is F₁ and when is it the wrong choice?
column2: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, high only when both are. It is wrong whenever you genuinely care more about one error type than the other — which is most of the time. Reaching for F₁ can be a way of avoiding a product decision.

column1: Why must you scale features before gradient descent?
column2: Unscaled features make the cost surface an elongated valley, so GD zig-zags and converges slowly. Scaled features make it a round bowl with a direct path. (The Normal Equation is unaffected.)

column1: Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch GD?
column2: Batch uses all instances per step — stable but slow, no out-of-core. Stochastic uses one — fast, noisy, escapes local minima, never settles without a decaying schedule. Mini-batch uses a small batch — the practical compromise, and it exploits GPU matrix ops.

column1: How do learning curves distinguish underfitting from overfitting?
column2: Both curves plateauing high and close together = underfitting (more data won't help). Low training error with a large gap to validation = overfitting (more data will help).

column1: Why does ℓ₁ (Lasso) produce exactly-zero weights while ℓ₂ (Ridge) does not?
column2: The ℓ₁ constraint region is a diamond whose corners lie on the axes, and optima tend to land on corners — a corner means some coordinate is exactly 0. ℓ₂'s region is a sphere with no corners, so it shrinks smoothly toward zero without reaching it.

column1: Write the softmax function and say why it matters for LLMs.
column2: p_k = exp(s_k) / Σ_j exp(s_j). An LLM's output layer is a softmax over the vocabulary — next-token prediction is softmax regression with K ≈ 50,000 classes, and temperature is a scalar dividing s_k before exponentiating.

column1: Why does log loss punish confident wrong answers so severely?
column2: The cost includes −log(p̂) for the true class, which goes to infinity as p̂ → 0. Predicting 0.001 for something that happens costs ~6.9; predicting 0.5 costs ~0.69.

column1: Ridge, Lasso, or Elastic Net?
column2: Ridge by default. Lasso when you believe only a few features matter (it selects them). Elastic Net over plain Lasso when features outnumber instances or several are strongly correlated, because Lasso behaves erratically there.

column1: What is a support vector?
column2: A training instance on or inside the margin street. Only these determine the decision boundary — all other instances could be moved (without crossing the margin) and the model would not change.

column1: Your SVM is overfitting. Which way do you move C and gamma?
column2: Decrease both. Lower C widens the street and allows more violations; lower gamma widens the RBF bell and smooths the boundary. Both are regularization knobs where smaller means more regularized.

column1: What is the kernel trick?
column2: A way to compute the dot product of two instances as if they had been projected into a very high-dimensional feature space, without ever computing that projection. It gives you the expressiveness of high-degree features at the cost of a similarity function.

column1: Why did kernel SVMs lose to neural networks on large datasets?
column2: SVC training is O(m²n) to O(m³n) in the number of instances, so it does not scale past ~100k rows and cannot train out-of-core. Neural networks train with mini-batch SGD, which is linear in data and streams.

column1: What does the CART algorithm optimize at each node?
column2: It greedily searches for the (feature, threshold) pair minimizing the size-weighted impurity of the two resulting children, then recurses. It never revisits a split — finding the globally optimal tree is NP-complete.

column1: Gini impurity vs entropy — which should you use?
column2: Rarely matters. Gini is slightly faster (no logarithm) and is the default; entropy tends to yield slightly more balanced trees. Not a decision worth agonizing over.

column1: Which hyperparameters regularize a decision tree, and in which direction?
column2: Increase the min_* parameters (min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf) and decrease the max_* ones (max_depth, max_leaf_nodes, max_features).

column1: Why are decision trees called high-variance models?
column2: Small changes in the training data produce a completely different tree structure. Ensembling (bagging, random forests) exploits exactly this: averaging many high-variance, low-bias models cancels the variance.

column1: What is the orthogonal-boundary limitation?
column2: Every CART split is axis-aligned, so a diagonal decision boundary must be approximated by a staircase. Rotating the data can turn a trivial problem into a convoluted tree; PCA sometimes fixes it.

column1: Why do ensembles work, and what is the necessary condition?
column2: Law of large numbers — many slightly-better-than-random voters aggregate to a much more accurate one. The condition is error independence: models must make different mistakes. Correlated models give no benefit.

column1: Bagging vs pasting?
column2: Bagging samples training subsets with replacement, pasting without. Bagging gives each predictor a more distorted view, so slightly higher bias but lower variance — usually preferred.

column1: What is out-of-bag (oob) evaluation?
column2: With bootstrap sampling each predictor sees only ~63% of instances (1 − 1/e). The unseen ~37% serve as a validation set for that predictor; averaging across the ensemble gives a free validation score with no separate holdout.

column1: How does a random forest add diversity beyond bagging?
column2: It also restricts each split to a random subset of features (max_features, default √n). Trees then disagree about which features to use, not just which rows they saw.

column1: AdaBoost vs gradient boosting — what does each new predictor learn from?
column2: AdaBoost re-weights the instances the previous predictors got wrong. Gradient boosting fits the new predictor directly to the residual errors of the ensemble so far.

column1: Why can't boosting be parallelized?
column2: It is sequential by definition — predictor n+1 is trained on the errors (or reweighted data) produced by predictor n. Bagging, by contrast, trains every predictor independently and scales across cores trivially.

column1: What LLM technique is ensemble voting in disguise?
column2: Self-consistency — sample the same prompt several times at nonzero temperature and take the majority answer. Also ensembles of LLM judges in evaluation.

column1: State the curse of dimensionality with a concrete number.
column2: Two random points in a unit square are ~0.52 apart on average; in a 1,000,000-dimensional unit hypercube, ~408.25. In high dimensions everything is far from everything, distances stop discriminating, and nearly all points sit near the boundary.

column1: What is the manifold hypothesis?
column2: Real high-dimensional data concentrates on a much lower-dimensional manifold — images of faces occupy a tiny structured region of all possible pixel arrays. The implicit second assumption, that the task is simpler on the manifold, is often but not always true.

column1: How does PCA choose its axes?
column2: The first component is the direction of maximum variance (equivalently, minimum squared projection distance); each subsequent component is orthogonal to the previous ones and captures the most remaining variance. Computed via SVD, on centered data.

column1: How do you choose the number of PCA components?
column2: By explained variance, not intuition: take the smallest d whose cumulative explained_variance_ratio_ reaches your target (commonly 95%). In scikit-learn, PCA(n_components=0.95) does it directly.

column1: What must you never conclude from a t-SNE or UMAP plot?
column2: That cluster sizes or the distances between clusters mean anything. Both are artifacts of the algorithm. These plots reveal that structure exists; they do not measure it.

column1: Why does embedding search use cosine similarity rather than Euclidean distance?
column2: In high dimensions Euclidean distances concentrate — everything is roughly equidistant — while angular relationships stay informative. Cosine also ignores magnitude, which for embeddings usually encodes frequency rather than meaning.

column1: Why can't you pick k by minimizing K-Means inertia?
column2: Inertia decreases monotonically with k and hits zero when every point is its own cluster. Use the elbow in the inertia curve, or better, the silhouette score / silhouette diagram.

column1: What is the silhouette coefficient?
column2: (b − a) / max(a, b), where a is the mean distance to points in the same cluster and b the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. Ranges −1 (wrong cluster) to +1 (well separated).

column1: Give three ways DBSCAN differs from K-Means.
column2: (1) No need to specify the number of clusters. (2) Finds arbitrarily-shaped clusters, not just spherical ones. (3) Explicitly labels outliers. Also: it has no predict method — fit a classifier on its labels to handle new points.

column1: What can a Gaussian Mixture Model do that K-Means cannot?
column2: Fit elliptical clusters of differing size, shape, density, and orientation (it estimates full covariance matrices); give soft probabilistic assignments; generate new samples; and provide a density estimate usable for anomaly detection.

column1: How do you choose the number of components for a GMM?
column2: Minimize BIC or AIC, which trade likelihood against parameter count. Alternatively use BayesianGaussianMixture, which drives unnecessary component weights to ~0 given an upper bound.

column1: What does clustering have to do with reducing labeling cost?
column2: Label one representative instance per cluster and propagate the label to the cluster. Géron's demo shows 50 well-chosen representatives massively outperforming 50 random labels — the core argument for active learning.

column1: What is backpropagation in one sentence?
column2: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation combined with gradient descent — a forward pass that caches intermediate activations, then a backward pass applying the chain rule from loss to parameters, then a gradient step.

column1: Why can't you initialize all neural network weights to zero?
column2: Every neuron in a layer would compute the same output and receive the same gradient, so they would stay identical forever — the layer collapses to a single neuron. Random initialization breaks the symmetry.

column1: Why must activation functions be nonlinear?
column2: Composing linear layers gives another linear layer: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. Without nonlinearity, any depth of network is equivalent to a single linear layer.

column1: Which output activation and loss for multiclass classification, and why does it matter for LLMs?
column2: Softmax output with categorical cross-entropy. This is exactly an LLM's output layer — next-token prediction is multiclass classification over the vocabulary.

column1: sparse_categorical_crossentropy vs categorical_crossentropy?
column2: Sparse takes integer class indices; the non-sparse version takes one-hot vectors. Using the wrong one gives a shape error or silently wrong training.

column1: How do you find a good learning rate?
column2: The LR-range test: ramp the learning rate exponentially during a short training run and plot the loss against it. Choose a value slightly below where the loss starts to climb.

column1: Why does training memory scale with activations rather than weights?
column2: Backprop needs the forward-pass activations to apply the chain rule, so they are all cached until the backward pass consumes them. This is the basis of fine-tuning memory math and of gradient-checkpointing as a mitigation.

column1: Why do gradients vanish in deep networks?
column2: Backprop multiplies many terms; if they are consistently < 1 the product approaches zero and lower layers stop learning. Historically caused by saturating sigmoid activations plus N(0,1) initialization, which grew activation variance until neurons saturated where the derivative is ~0.

column1: Which initialization for which activation?
column2: Glorot/Xavier for tanh, sigmoid, softmax, and linear. He for ReLU and its variants. LeCun for SELU.

column1: What does batch normalization do, and what are γ and β?
column2: It normalizes each layer's inputs to zero mean and unit variance over the mini-batch, then rescales with learned γ (scale) and β (shift). The learned parameters mean the network can undo the normalization, so no expressiveness is lost.

column1: Why do transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm?
column2: LayerNorm normalizes across features within a single example, so it is independent of batch size and of other sequences in the batch. That matters for variable-length text and for inference at batch size 1, where BatchNorm's batch statistics are unusable.

column1: What is a dying ReLU and how do you fix it?
column2: A neuron whose weighted sum is always negative outputs 0 and receives gradient 0, so it never recovers. Fix with Leaky ReLU, ELU, or SELU, which have a nonzero slope for negative inputs.

column1: What is the transfer-learning recipe?
column2: Freeze the reused layers, train the new output layer to convergence, then unfreeze the top one or two reused layers and continue with a ~10× lower learning rate. In Keras you must recompile after changing trainable.

column1: Why does LLM training use learning-rate warmup?
column2: Adam's moment estimates are unreliable during the first few hundred steps; applying the full learning rate then can destabilize training permanently. Warmup ramps the rate up gradually, then cosine decay anneals it.

column1: What is AdamW and why did it replace Adam for transformers?
column2: Adam with decoupled weight decay. Adam's L2 penalty interacts badly with its per-parameter adaptive scaling, so the effective regularization varies by parameter. AdamW applies decay separately from the adaptive step.

column1: What is the difference between a loss and a metric?
column2: A loss must be differentiable because gradients flow through it, and need not be human-interpretable. A metric need not be differentiable and should be interpretable. Metrics are also streamed — accumulated across batches, not averaged per batch.

column1: What does a GradientTape do?
column2: Records every operation involving watched tensors during the forward pass, then replays that graph in reverse to compute gradients. Variables are watched automatically; constants need tape.watch(). The tape is released after one gradient() call unless persistent=True.

column1: Write the universal training loop in five steps.
column2: Forward pass → compute loss → backward pass for gradients → optimizer step → reset gradients. Identical in TF (tape.gradient / apply_gradients) and PyTorch (loss.backward() / optimizer.step() / zero_grad()).

column1: Why should you use the framework's cross_entropy instead of composing log(softmax(x))?
column2: Numerical stability. The naive composition overflows or underflows for large or small logits; the fused implementation uses the log-sum-exp trick internally.

column1: What happens to plain Python code inside a @tf.function?
column2: It executes only once, at trace time, and its effects are baked into the graph. print() fires once; tf.print() fires every call. Python loops over Python data are unrolled.

column1: What does tf.stop_gradient (PyTorch: .detach()) do, and where is it used?
column2: Blocks gradient flow through part of the graph. Used for freezing layers, straight-through estimators, target networks in RL, and anywhere you want a value without a gradient path.

column1: What does prefetch do and why does it matter so much?
column2: While the GPU trains on batch n, the CPU prepares batch n+1, overlapping the two instead of alternating idle periods. It is frequently a ~2× throughput win for one line of code.

column1: Why does the shuffle buffer size matter?
column2: shuffle samples from a fixed-size buffer, not the whole dataset. If the data has any ordering (e.g. sorted by class) and the buffer is small, batches will be non-representative — often single-class — and training will fail in ways that look like model bugs.

column1: One-hot encoding vs embeddings for categorical features?
column2: One-hot for small vocabularies: sparse, orthogonal, no similarity structure. Embeddings for large ones: a dense trainable vector per category (typically 10–300 dims), learned by gradient descent, in which semantic similarity emerges rather than being specified.

column1: What is an Embedding layer, mechanically?
column2: A trainable lookup table — a (vocab_size, dim) matrix where embedding(i) returns row i. An LLM's token embedding layer is exactly this; GPT-2 small's is (50257, 768).

column1: What is training/serving skew, and how do you prevent it?
column2: Preprocessing at serving time drifts from preprocessing at training time, so the model sees differently-transformed inputs in production. Nothing crashes; quality just degrades. Prevent it by putting preprocessing inside the model as layers, so it ships with the weights.

column1: Why shard data into a few large files instead of millions of small ones?
column2: Per-file filesystem overhead dominates read time for small files. Large sequential shards read far faster and can be read in parallel across shards. TFRecord, Parquet, and WebDataset all exist for this reason.

column1: What two constraints does a CNN impose on a dense layer, and what do they buy?
column2: Locality (each neuron sees only a small receptive field) and weight sharing (the same filter slides everywhere). They buy an enormous reduction in parameters and translation equivariance.

column1: Why prefer two stacked 3×3 convolutions over one 5×5?
column2: Same receptive field, fewer parameters (2×9=18 vs 25 per channel pair), and an extra nonlinearity between them, so more expressive power for less cost.

column1: What problem do residual (skip) connections solve, and how?
column2: Vanishing gradients in very deep networks. The block learns f(x) = h(x) − x and outputs f(x) + x, giving gradients a direct path backwards and making an untrained block an identity function — so adding depth never hurts at initialization.

column1: Where do residual connections appear in a transformer?
column2: The whole block: x = x + attention(norm(x)) then x = x + ffn(norm(x)). The x carried through those additions is what interpretability work calls the residual stream.

column1: Why does CNN training run out of memory, and what do you change first?
column2: Activation memory, not weights — backprop caches every layer's activations for the backward pass, and it scales with batch size. Reduce the batch size first.

column1: What is inductive bias, with CNNs and transformers as the contrast?
column2: The assumptions an architecture encodes. CNNs assume locality and translation invariance, so they learn efficiently from little data on images. Transformers assume almost nothing, so they need far more data — and surpass CNNs once they have it.

column1: What is a 1×1 convolution for?
column2: It has no spatial extent, so it acts purely across channels — a learned linear mixing of feature maps, typically used as a cheap dimensionality bottleneck (GoogLeNet, ResNet bottleneck blocks).

column1: Why can't RNN training be parallelized over time?
column2: The hidden state at step t depends on step t−1, so steps must run in order. Sequence length becomes sequential wall-clock time regardless of hardware. Self-attention removes this by computing all positions simultaneously as one matrix multiply.

column1: What are an LSTM's three gates?
column2: Forget (what to erase from the cell state), input (what new information to write), and output (what part of the cell state to expose at this step). The cell state itself flows through with only multiplicative and additive interactions — a memory highway.

column1: Why do RNNs use tanh rather than ReLU by default?
column2: The same weights are applied repeatedly through time, so an unbounded activation compounds and explodes. A saturating activation keeps the recurrence stable.

column1: Why LayerNorm rather than BatchNorm in an RNN?
column2: BatchNorm's statistics are computed across the batch and do not behave sensibly across time steps or variable-length sequences. LayerNorm normalizes within a single example, so it is independent of batch composition — the same reason transformers use it.

column1: What is a dilated causal convolution, and what does WaveNet do with it?
column2: A 1D convolution that skips inputs at a fixed rate and only looks backwards in time. WaveNet doubles the dilation each layer (1, 2, 4, 8, …), so 10 layers reach a 1,024-step receptive field — with fully parallel training and no recurrence.

column1: What lesson does WaveNet beating LSTMs teach about architecture?
column2: The winning move was not better recurrence but removing recurrence, so training could parallelize. Attention took the same step further, which is why transformers replaced RNNs.

column1: What problem does attention solve in seq2seq models?
column2: The fixed-size context-vector bottleneck. Rather than compressing the whole input into one vector, the decoder computes a fresh weighted combination of all encoder outputs at every output step, so translation quality no longer collapses on long sentences.

column1: Write scaled dot-product attention and name each term.
column2: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V. Query = what this position seeks; Key = what each position offers; Value = what each contributes when selected. The softmax turns scores into weights summing to 1; the result is a weighted average of values.

column1: Why divide by √d_k in attention?
column2: For large d_k, dot products of random vectors have variance proportional to d_k, so the scores get large and push the softmax into saturation, where one weight is ~1 and gradients vanish. Dividing by √d_k restores variance ~1.

column1: Why is multi-head attention better than a single attention operation?
column2: One attention op produces exactly one weighted average, so it can attend to only one thing. Multiple heads attend in different learned subspaces simultaneously — one may track syntactic agreement while another tracks coreference.

column1: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
column2: Self-attention is permutation-invariant — it treats the input as a set. Without explicit position information the model cannot distinguish "dog bites man" from "man bites dog."

column1: What does temperature do, mechanically?
column2: Divides the logits by T before the softmax. T < 1 sharpens the distribution toward the argmax (conservative); T > 1 flattens it toward uniform (diverse). It is applied to logits, not to probabilities.

column1: Self-attention vs cross-attention?
column2: In self-attention, Q, K, and V all come from the same sequence. In cross-attention, Q comes from the decoder while K and V come from the encoder — which is how a decoder consults the source sentence.

column1: Why does an autoencoder need a bottleneck (or equivalent regularization)?
column2: Without one it can learn the identity function and copy input to output, learning nothing. Constraining capacity forces it to discard information, and what it chooses to keep is the useful representation.

column1: What classical technique does a linear autoencoder with MSE loss reproduce?
column2: PCA. Adding nonlinear layers generalizes it to nonlinear dimensionality reduction, capable of unrolling manifolds a linear projection cannot.

column1: What is a denoising autoencoder, and which famous LLM training objective is it?
column2: Corrupt the input (noise or dropout) and train to reconstruct the clean original. BERT's masked language modeling is exactly this — masking is the corruption, and the original tokens are the target.

column1: What does the KL divergence term do in a VAE?
column2: It pushes the encoded distributions toward a standard Gaussian, making the latent space smooth and continuous. Without it, codings scatter arbitrarily and points between them decode to nothing — so you cannot sample or interpolate.

column1: What is the reparameterization trick and why is it needed?
column2: Sample ε ~ N(0,1) and compute μ + σ·ε instead of sampling directly from N(μ, σ). It moves the randomness outside the computation graph so gradients can flow through what would otherwise be a non-differentiable random node.

column1: What is mode collapse in a GAN?
column2: The generator discovers one (or a few) outputs that reliably fool the discriminator and produces only those, losing all diversity. The loss curves can look healthy throughout, which is why you must inspect samples.

column1: Why are sparse autoencoders suddenly relevant to LLM interpretability?
column2: Trained on transformer activations, they decompose superposed polysemantic neurons into sparse, more monosemantic features — the main current technique for reading what an LLM has internally represented.

column1: What is the credit assignment problem?
column2: Rewards are delayed and aggregate, so it is unclear which of the many actions taken deserve credit. Discounting (γ) and advantage estimation are the standard partial answers. In RLHF, one scalar reward must be attributed across hundreds of token decisions.

column1: Why normalize returns in policy gradient methods?
column2: Without a baseline, every action in a successful episode is reinforced — including the bad ones. Subtracting the mean makes the signal relative (an advantage), so only better-than-average actions get positive weight, drastically reducing variance.

column1: Map RL vocabulary onto RLHF.
column2: Agent = the LLM; action = emitting a token; policy = the next-token distribution; environment = the conversation; reward = a reward model trained on human preferences; policy gradient = PPO. DPO skips the RL loop by optimizing a preference objective directly.

column1: Why does a DQN need a replay buffer and a target network?
column2: Consecutive experiences are highly correlated, violating SGD's IID assumption — the replay buffer decorrelates them. And the regression target moves as you update the network, so you chase your own tail — a periodically-frozen target network stabilizes it.

column1: What is reward hacking, and why does it matter for LLMs?
column2: The agent optimizes the reward you specified rather than the outcome you intended, exploiting flaws in the proxy. Reward models in RLHF are proxies for human preference; optimizing hard against them finds their failure modes — which is why a KL penalty to the reference model is used.

column1: What statistical bias does Double DQN correct, and where else does it appear?
column2: Taking the max over noisy estimates is biased upward, so plain Q-learning overestimates values. The same bias makes best-of-n selection overestimate quality when the selector is a noisy judge — a real hazard in LLM evaluation.

column1: What does a SavedModel contain, and why does that matter?
column2: The computation graph, the weights, and any preprocessing layers. Bundling preprocessing is what prevents training/serving skew — the transformation ships with the weights instead of being reimplemented in the serving code.

column1: What is post-training quantization and what does it buy?
column2: Storing weights as 8-bit integers (with a per-tensor scale and zero-point) instead of 32-bit floats. Roughly 4× smaller and often faster, at a small accuracy cost. This is the same mechanism behind 4-bit quantized LLMs.

column1: Mirrored strategy vs parameter server — what's the tradeoff?
column2: Mirrored is synchronous: all replicas AllReduce their gradients and apply identical updates — correct, but the slowest worker sets the pace. Parameter server is asynchronous: no stragglers, but replicas compute on stale parameters, which often converges worse.

column1: Why was model parallelism "usually not worth it" for CNNs but mandatory for LLMs?
column2: CNNs fit on one device, so splitting them added communication for no benefit. A 70B-parameter model simply does not fit, so tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism are combined out of necessity — plus ZeRO/FSDP sharding of optimizer state.

column1: What are canary, A/B, and shadow deployments?
column2: Canary routes a small traffic percentage to the new version and ramps up on good metrics. A/B splits traffic deliberately to compare. Shadow sends real traffic to the new version but discards its responses, comparing offline — the safest option.

column1: Why does server-side batching help, and what does it cost?
column2: Grouping concurrent requests into one inference call greatly improves hardware utilization. It costs a little latency, since early requests wait for the batch to fill. Max batch size and max wait time are the knobs — and this is the direct ancestor of continuous batching in LLM serving.

column1: What is word2vec's fundamental limitation?
column2: One static vector per word regardless of context — "bank" gets a single embedding serving both the riverbank and the financial institution. Contextual embeddings from transformers give each occurrence its own vector.

column1: Encoder-only vs decoder-only models — what determines what each can do?
column2: Encoder-only (BERT) uses bidirectional attention and is trained by masked language modeling — great for classification and retrieval, incapable of generation. Decoder-only (GPT) uses causal attention and next-token prediction — built for generation.

column1: What is the difference between a base model and an instruct model?
column2: A base model is pretrained only and continues text; asked to "write a poem," it may produce more instructions because that is a plausible continuation. An instruct model has been post-trained (SFT + preference tuning) to treat the text as a request.

column1: Why does skipping the chat template hurt quality?
column2: Instruct models are fine-tuned with specific role and turn markers. Feeding a raw string puts the model off-distribution from its training format. Use tokenizer.apply_chat_template().

column1: What makes LLMs broadly useful in a way earlier NLP models were not?
column2: Generality. One model performs classification, extraction, summarization, translation, and generation with no task-specific training, because all of those tasks can be expressed as text continuation.

column1: How does Byte Pair Encoding build its vocabulary?
column2: Start from individual characters/bytes, repeatedly count adjacent pairs in the corpus and merge the most frequent pair into a new token, until reaching the target vocabulary size. Frequent words become single tokens; rare words stay split.

column1: Why can't an LLM count the letters in a word?
column2: It never sees letters. "strawberry" arrives as something like ["straw", "berry"] — two integers. Counting characters requires introspecting a representation the model does not have.

column1: Why does the same sentence cost more tokens in Thai than in English?
column2: The tokenizer's vocabulary was learned from a mostly-English corpus, so other languages fragment into many more subword pieces. The cost difference can be 3–5×, which is a real production concern for multilingual apps.

column1: What is the difference between the embedding matrix and contextual embeddings?
column2: The embedding matrix is a static lookup table (vocab_size × dim) — one context-free vector per token ID. Contextual embeddings are what each position holds after passing through the transformer's layers, shaped by surrounding tokens. Both exist in the same model.

column1: Why does word2vec need negative sampling?
column2: Without negatives the classifier trivially answers "related" to everything and all vectors collapse to one point. Contrast between real neighbours and random words is what creates the geometric structure.

column1: Why shouldn't you mean-pool a generative LLM's token vectors for semantic search?
column2: Those representations were optimized for next-token prediction, not for cosine similarity between whole texts. Embedding models are trained with a contrastive objective specifically to make that similarity meaningful.

column1: Why do "the" and " the" behave differently in a prompt?
column2: In most BPE tokenizers the leading space is part of the token, so they are two distinct IDs. This is why trailing whitespace in a prompt can measurably change model output.

column1: What are the two operations in a transformer block, and how do they differ?
column2: Attention moves information between positions; the feedforward network processes each position independently. Attention is the only place cross-position information flows. Both are wrapped in residual connections around a layer norm.

column1: What is the residual stream?
column2: The x carried through x = x + attention(norm(x)) and x = x + ffn(norm(x)) — a shared bus running the depth of the network that each block reads from and writes an update into. It also gives gradients a direct path to the embeddings.

column1: What is the KV cache and why is it valid?
column2: During generation, the keys and values for earlier positions depend only on tokens already fixed, so they never change. Caching them means each new token computes only its own Q/K/V and attends over cached history, instead of re-running the whole prefix.

column1: Why are prefill and decode bounded by different resources?
column2: Prefill processes the entire prompt in parallel — lots of arithmetic on lots of data, so it is compute-bound. Decode produces one token at a time, reading the whole model and KV cache per token, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound.

column1: Why is attention quadratic, and why does it matter?
column2: The score matrix is n × n for a sequence of n tokens, so compute and memory scale with n². Doubling context quadruples the cost — the reason FlashAttention, GQA, and sliding-window attention exist.

column1: What does FlashAttention change?
column2: None of the mathematics — the output is identical. It is an IO-aware tiled implementation that never materializes the full n×n matrix in slow HBM, keeping tiles in fast SRAM instead. A pure memory-hierarchy win.

column1: What is GQA and what does it trade?
column2: Grouped-query attention: groups of query heads share a single key/value head. It shrinks the KV cache substantially (the main serving bottleneck) for a small quality cost, and is the current standard — between full MHA and the more aggressive MQA.

column1: What does RoPE do differently from additive positional encodings?
column2: It rotates the query and key vectors by an angle proportional to position, so their dot product depends on relative distance rather than absolute position. This matches what language actually needs and extrapolates better to longer contexts.

column1: Roughly where do a transformer's parameters live?
column2: About two-thirds in the feedforward networks, the rest in attention projections and embeddings. Evidence suggests the FFN acts as a key-value memory for factual associations, which is why knowledge-editing research targets it.

column1: What are the four ways to classify text with modern models?
column2: (1) An existing task-specific fine-tuned model; (2) frozen embeddings + a trained classifier; (3) zero-shot via similarity to embedded label descriptions; (4) prompting a generative model. Cost spans about three orders of magnitude.

column1: Why should embeddings + logistic regression be your default text classifier?
column2: Trains in seconds on CPU from a few hundred examples, deterministic, cheap at inference, versionable, and it gives you a probability — so you get a real precision/recall curve and a tunable threshold. It is also the baseline that tells you whether anything fancier was worth it.

column1: What control do you lose when classifying with a generative model?
column2: The threshold. You get a label, not a calibrated score, so you cannot dial in a specific precision or recall operating point without asking for logprobs. You also lose determinism and pay far more per call.

column1: How does zero-shot classification with embeddings work?
column2: Embed descriptions of each label as if they were documents, embed the input, and assign the label with the highest cosine similarity. Quality is sensitive to label phrasing — "A negative review" beats "negative".

column1: What are the four stages of the BERTopic pipeline?
column2: Embed (SBERT) → reduce dimensionality (UMAP) → cluster (HDBSCAN) → label (c-TF-IDF, optionally refined by an LLM). Every stage is independently swappable — it is a framework, not an algorithm.

column1: Why reduce to 5–15 dimensions rather than 2 before clustering?
column2: 2D is for visualization and discards far too much structure. Density-based clustering needs meaningful density, which 2D projection destroys — but full 384/768-dim space suffers the curse of dimensionality. 5–15 is the working range.

column1: Why HDBSCAN rather than K-Means for topic modeling?
column2: It does not require you to specify the number of topics (which you cannot know), handles clusters of varying density, and labels documents that belong to no topic as noise (−1) rather than forcing them into a cluster.

column1: What is c-TF-IDF?
column2: TF-IDF applied at cluster level: concatenate all documents in a cluster into one meta-document, then find terms distinctive to that cluster relative to other clusters. It yields cheap, deterministic, interpretable topic keywords.

column1: What is MMR and where else does it appear?
column2: Maximal marginal relevance — select items that are relevant and mutually diverse. Used here to avoid five synonyms in a topic label, and in RAG to avoid retrieving five near-identical chunks.

column1: What does temperature do mechanically?
column2: Divides the logits by T before the softmax. T < 1 sharpens the distribution toward the argmax; T > 1 flattens it toward uniform. It changes randomness, never competence.

column1: Why is top-p usually preferable to top-k?
column2: top-k always keeps k candidates regardless of confidence, so when the model is certain it still admits k−1 bad options. top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p, adapting to the distribution's shape.

column1: Why does chain-of-thought prompting improve accuracy?
column2: The model generates tokens sequentially, each conditioned on the previous. Reasoning tokens enter the context and effectively give the model more computation before committing to an answer. It cannot reason "in its head" — there is only the sequence.

column1: What classical ML technique is self-consistency, and when does it fail?
column2: Ensembling by majority vote, with temperature providing the diversity. It corrects random error but not systematic bias — a model that is confidently wrong will produce the same wrong answer n times at n× the cost.

column1: What is constrained (grammar-based) decoding and why is it stronger than asking for JSON?
column2: It masks the logits at each step so only tokens valid under a grammar can be sampled. Invalid output is unreachable rather than merely discouraged. Asking nicely fails eventually; this cannot.

column1: Is temperature=0 deterministic?
column2: Approximately, not guaranteed. Floating-point non-associativity in batched GPU kernels and varying batch composition between requests produce occasional variation. Never build a system requiring bit-identical output.

column1: Why does a chatbot need memory management at all?
column2: LLM APIs are stateless — the model retains nothing between calls. The illusion of conversation exists only because you resend the history each turn, which costs tokens and eventually overflows the context window.

column1: Compare the four conversation memory strategies.
column2: Full buffer (perfect fidelity, unbounded cost); windowed buffer (bounded, loses anything older than k turns); summary (bounded, lossy and compounding); vector retrieval (bounded, retrieves relevant history but loses continuity).

column1: What actually happens when an LLM "calls a tool"?
column2: It emits text or a structured function-call object describing the desired call. Your code parses it, validates it, executes it, and inserts the result back into the context. The model is the decision-maker; the harness does everything else — including all authorization.

column1: Why does error compounding matter in multi-step LLM systems?
column2: Success rates multiply. Four steps at 90% each give 66% end to end; ten steps at 95% give 60%. This is the central constraint on agent reliability and the reason to measure end-to-end rather than per-step.

column1: What is the ReAct pattern?
column2: A loop that interleaves reasoning traces with actions: think about what to do, act by calling a tool, observe the result, repeat. The explicit reasoning both improves decisions and makes the trajectory debuggable.

column1: Why doesn't dense retrieval replace keyword search?
column2: Dense retrieval matches meaning, so it fails on exact strings — error codes, IDs, rare product names, specific numbers. BM25 finds those instantly. Hybrid retrieval with rank fusion is the production default.

column1: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?
column2: A bi-encoder embeds query and document separately, so document vectors are precomputable and search is fast — but the two never interact until a final dot product. A cross-encoder processes them together with full attention across both: far more accurate, far too slow for a whole corpus.

column1: What is the two-stage retrieval pattern and why is it high-leverage?
column2: Retrieve 50–100 candidates with the fast bi-encoder, then rerank them with a slow cross-encoder and keep the top 3–5. It gets cross-encoder accuracy at bi-encoder cost, and it is the cheapest large improvement to a naive RAG system.

column1: Why does chunk overlap matter?
column2: Without it, an answer spanning a chunk boundary is split so that neither chunk contains it completely — making it effectively unretrievable. 10–20% overlap is typical.

column1: Name five RAG failure modes.
column2: Retrieval miss (the answer was never retrieved — the most common); distraction from irrelevant chunks; lost-in-the-middle positional weakness; the model ignoring context in favor of parametric knowledge; and conflicting retrieved sources.

column1: Why evaluate retrieval and generation separately?
column2: Retrieval has ground truth — did the right chunk come back? — and is measurable with recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG. Generation quality is much harder to measure. End-to-end scores alone never tell you which half to fix.

column1: What is the query/passage prefix trap?
column2: Many retrieval models are asymmetric and are trained expecting "query: " on queries and "passage: " on documents. Omitting the prefixes degrades results substantially, and it fails silently.

column1: How does a Vision Transformer feed an image to a transformer?
column2: Cut the image into fixed patches (e.g. 16×16 pixels), flatten and linearly project each patch to d_model, add positional embeddings, and treat the result as a token sequence. A patch is a token.

column1: How is CLIP trained?
column2: Two encoders (image and text) trained contrastively on (image, caption) pairs. Within a batch of N pairs, the N diagonal similarities are positives and the N²−N off-diagonal ones are negatives, with symmetric cross-entropy. Large batches matter because the batch supplies the negatives.

column1: How do you give a language model vision without retraining it?
column2: Take a pretrained vision encoder and a pretrained LLM, freeze both, and train only a projection layer that maps image embeddings into the LLM's token embedding space. Projected image vectors are then fed as if they were token embeddings.

column1: Why does "a photo of a cat" beat "cat" for CLIP zero-shot classification?
column2: CLIP was trained on image–caption pairs, so full caption-like sentences match its training distribution. Bare label words are off-distribution. It is prompt engineering applied to images.

column1: What is the recurring contrastive-learning recipe across word2vec, CLIP, and sentence embeddings?
column2: Define positive pairs, sample or mine negatives, and train so positives are close and negatives far in a shared space. The differences are only in what counts as a pair and where the negatives come from.

column1: Why is a generative LLM's hidden state a poor sentence embedding?
column2: It was optimized for next-token prediction, an objective that never asks for cosine similarity between whole texts to be meaningful. Embedding models are trained specifically so that similarity in the space means semantic similarity.

column1: How does MultipleNegativesRankingLoss work?
column2: Given a batch of (anchor, positive) pairs, every other positive in the batch serves as a negative for the current anchor, with cross-entropy over the similarities. It needs only positive pairs, and larger batches supply more negatives — so batch size is a quality hyperparameter.

column1: What is a hard negative and why does it matter?
column2: A plausible-but-wrong document — for "reset my password", a doc about resetting your username. Random negatives are trivially separable and quickly stop producing gradient; hard negatives are where the model learns the actual decision boundary.

column1: What is the danger of aggressive hard-negative mining?
column2: False negatives — mined documents that are genuinely relevant but unlabeled. Training on those teaches the model to push away correct answers. Mitigate by skipping the top ranks or filtering candidates with a cross-encoder.

column1: How does SimCSE create positive pairs without any labels?
column2: Pass the same sentence through the encoder twice with different dropout masks. The two slightly different vectors form a positive pair — a training signal manufactured from unlabeled text.

column1: Why is MTEB rank a poor way to choose an embedding model?
column2: Benchmark performance does not predict performance on your domain, especially for jargon-heavy or non-English corpora. Fifty hand-labeled (query, relevant doc) pairs from your own data decide better than any leaderboard.

column1: What learning rate should you use to fine-tune a pretrained encoder, and why?
column2: 2e-5 to 5e-5 — roughly two orders of magnitude below training from scratch. The pretrained weights are already good; large updates destroy them (catastrophic forgetting).

column1: How does SetFit work?
column2: (1) Generate contrastive pairs from few labels — same-label pairs are positives, different-label pairs are negatives, so 16 examples yield hundreds of pairs. (2) Fine-tune a sentence embedder on those pairs. (3) Train a logistic-regression head on the resulting embeddings.

column1: What is SetFit's transferable insight?
column2: Turning a classification problem into a similarity problem multiplies your labeled data combinatorially, because pairs are quadratic in examples.

column1: When should you do continued MLM pretraining?
column2: When your domain is far from the pretraining corpus (clinical, legal, internal jargon) and you have far more unlabeled domain text than labels. MLM needs no labels, so it converts the resource you have into the improvement you need.

column1: Why does freezing lower layers help on small datasets?
column2: Lower layers encode general language features that transfer; upper layers are task-specific. Freezing the bottom reduces trainable parameters, which regularizes and prevents overfitting when data is scarce.

column1: Token masking vs whole-word masking in MLM?
column2: Token masking hides individual subword tokens; whole-word masking hides all subword pieces of a word together. Whole-word is harder and generally better, because it stops the model reconstructing a word from its own surviving fragments.

column1: Why does full fine-tuning of a 7B model need ~90 GB?
column2: 14 GB weights (fp16) + 14 GB gradients + ~56 GB Adam optimizer states (two fp32 moments per parameter) + activations. The optimizer states dominate, which is why PEFT methods target trainable parameter count specifically.

column1: What is LoRA's core idea?
column2: The weight update during fine-tuning has low intrinsic rank, so freeze W and learn W' = W + BA where B is d×r, A is r×k, and r ≪ min(d,k). For a 4096×4096 matrix at r=8, 16.7M parameters become 65k — about 0.4%.

column1: Why is LoRA's B matrix initialized to zero?
column2: So that BA = 0 at initialization and the adapted model starts out behaving exactly like the base model. A is initialized randomly to break symmetry; if both were zero, nothing would ever learn.

column1: What does QLoRA add, and what does it cost?
column2: A 4-bit NF4-quantized frozen base with bf16 compute, double quantization, and paged optimizers — putting a 7B fine-tune on a 16 GB GPU. It costs some speed (on-the-fly dequantization) and a small amount of quality versus fp16 LoRA.

column1: What is DPO and why did it displace PPO-based RLHF for most teams?
column2: Direct Preference Optimization trains on (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples with a loss that raises the chosen response's relative likelihood, constrained against a frozen reference model. No reward model, no RL loop — far simpler and cheaper to get working.

column1: Why must you mask the loss on prompt tokens during SFT?
column2: Otherwise the model is trained to reproduce instructions as well as responses. You want it to learn to generate the completion, so loss should apply only to response tokens.

column1: Should you fine-tune to add new factual knowledge?
column2: No. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour, format, and style; RAG supplies facts. Injecting knowledge by fine-tuning is expensive, unreliable, hard to update, and gives you no citations.
